sources.title: Pit River Tribe v. Bureau of Land Management — opinion filed September 19, 2019
sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit · National Indian Law Library transcription
sources.annotation: Primary judicial opinion on twenty-six unproven geothermal leases at Medicine Lake Highlands. The synopsis, background, procedural history, statutory discussion, and disposition were inspected for the narrow leasing holding: one productive lease did not justify the disputed forty-year continuation of all the others. The opinion distinguishes that issue from environmental-review and trust claims; it is not a judgment restoring tribal ownership or deciding every cultural-rights question. The library provides the opinion text openly despite the introductory Westlaw citation notice.

sources.title: Proclamation on the Establishment of the Sáttítla Highlands National Monument
sources.publisher: President Joseph R. Biden Jr. · archived White House
sources.annotation: Primary January 14, 2025 designation, inspected for its account of Pit River and neighboring peoples, volcanic groundwater, obsidian exchange, boundaries, and management provisions. It reserves approximately 224,676 acres of federal land and directs Forest Service consultation and opportunities for tribal co-stewardship and customary uses. Those directions are not evidence that a management plan or commission has been completed, nor a transfer of land title. The frozen presidential archive documents the 2025 action rather than every subsequent policy development. Sensitive site locations are not reproduced here.

sections.title: Using the courts to protect Medicine Lake Highlands
sections.text: The Pit River Tribe and allied organizations challenged federal decisions extending geothermal leases at Medicine Lake Highlands. In September 2019 the Ninth Circuit affirmed a ruling against the disputed forty-year continuation of twenty-six unproven leases based on a single proven lease in their unit. The case shows sustained tribal use of federal litigation, but its precise holding concerns the leasing statute. It should not be described as a ruling that returned the highlands to tribal ownership or settled all religious-freedom and environmental questions.

sections.title: Sáttítla designation and the work of stewardship
sections.text: On January 14, 2025, a presidential proclamation established Sáttítla Highlands National Monument on approximately 224,676 acres of federal land. Its account connects Pit River and Modoc homelands, wider Indigenous relationships, obsidian exchange, and groundwater moving through volcanic rock. The proclamation assigns management to the Forest Service and directs consultation, customary-use access, and opportunities for tribal co-stewardship. These are provisions of the designation; they do not establish completed implementation or a transfer of the entire homeland into tribal ownership. Tracking subsequent management decisions remains part of the research.
